title: Cusco (Qusqu)
summary: Cusco, in Peru's southern Andes at about 3,400 m, grew from a Killke-period town into the 15th-century capital of Tawantinsuyu, the Inca Empire; Spanish forces took it in 1533 and raised a colonial city on its Inca walls.
card: Killke-period communities lived in the Cuzco Basin before the Inca made it their seat. In the 15th century, traditionally under Pachacuti, the town was replanned as the sacred and political centre of Tawantinsuyu, with the Coricancha temple, royal compounds around the great plaza, Saqsaywaman on the hill above, and roads leaving for the empire's four quarters. After 1533 the Spanish divided the palaces into house plots and set churches and convents on Inca foundations, creating the layered city UNESCO inscribed in 1983.
what:
Cusco lies in a fertile valley of the southern Peruvian Andes at roughly 3,400 m above sea level. UNESCO notes more than 3,000 years of occupation in the valley before the Inca. In the Late Intermediate Period (c. 1000–1400 CE) the Cuzco Basin was home to communities using Killke-style pottery, and excavations beneath the modern streets show a Killke settlement that predates the Inca capital. Inca tradition traced the ruling line to Manco Capac, a mythical first ruler said to have come out of a cave at Tambotoco near Pacariqtambo; that story is recorded here as belief, not as an event.

In the 15th century the town was redesigned as the capital of Tawantinsuyu, the Inca state of four united parts. Colonial chronicles credit Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui, whose accession they date to 1438, with planning one urban whole running from the river confluence at Pumachupan up to Saqsaywaman. Its sacred core was the Coricancha, the Temple of the Sun, entered from the plaza of Intipampa. Royal compounds such as Cassana and Amarucancha faced the great plaza of Haukaypata, and the Acllahuasi housed the acllas, women chosen for religious service. Roads of the Qhapaq Ñan left the main plaza for the four suyus: Chinchaysuyu, Antisuyu, Collasuyu and Kuntisuyu.

Spanish forces under Francisco Pizarro entered the city on 15 November 1533 (Julian calendar). In 1534 the new Spanish municipality handed out house plots inside the royal compounds. In May 1536 Manco Inca laid siege to the city; heated sling-stones set its thatch roofs on fire and his forces held Saqsaywaman until the Spanish retook it, but the siege failed. In the 16th and 17th centuries churches and convents rose on Inca foundations, among them Santo Domingo over the Coricancha and Santa Catalina over the Acllahuasi. Earthquakes in 1650 and 1950 badly damaged the colonial city. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage property in 1983.

The timing of the imperial city is debated: chronicles put Pachacuti's rise at 1438, while radiocarbon dates from Machu Picchu and Inca provincial sites point to imperial activity several decades earlier.

uncertainty.note: Start is the beginning of the Late Intermediate Period (c. 1000 CE), when Killke-style pottery marks settlement in the Cuzco Basin (Covey et al. 2025); the Smithsonian places the Inca rise in Cusco in the early 1200s, and UNESCO counts more than 3,000 years of earlier occupation in the valley. The city is inhabited to the present, so the end is the current year. Dates of Inca reigns rest on a chronicle chronology that radiocarbon dating suggests is several decades too late.

how: Cusco became a capital through a long process. Late Intermediate Period communities built up the basin's settlements, and Covey and others argue that Inca state formation unfolded over generations of regional change rather than starting with one ruler. In the 15th century the town was rebuilt on a single plan, which the chronicles attribute to Pachacuti. The city was split into Hanan (upper) and Hurin (lower) Qosqo, and each half matched two of the empire's quarters: Chinchaysuyu and Antisuyu belonged to Hanan, Collasuyu and Kuntisuyu to Hurin. Ritual roads began at the Coricancha, and the trunk roads to the suyus started from the main plaza, tying the provinces to the centre. Builders used finely fitted granite and andesite for temples and royal compounds. At Saqsaywaman three terraced zigzag walls, pierced by fifteen gates, used blocks estimated at 90 to 125 tonnes. These walls were still being built when the Spanish arrived. After 1534 the Spanish kept the street grid, gave themselves 200-foot plots in the royal compounds, and moved Inca families out to outlying barrios. Parishes recorded from 1559–1560 were used to evangelise the native population and to resettle it in those barrios. The campaign against Andean religion destroyed shrines (huacas), and churches went up on Inca sacred sites. Earthquakes then reshaped the colonial fabric: an archaeoseismic survey logged almost 3,000 damage features at nine Inca sites. It recognised two strong shaking events at Cusco and argued that one struck during Inca times (c. 1400–1533). The 1950 earthquake, by contrast, did little harm to Inca masonry.
why_it_matters: Cusco was the political and sacred centre of the largest state of the pre-Columbian Americas. The Qhapaq Ñan was laid out to start from its main plaza, so the roads, waystations and shrines of Tawantinsuyu tied every province back to the capital and its ruler. That made the city the decisive prize of the Spanish invasion. Its capture in November 1533 handed the invaders the seat of Andean authority. When Manco Inca's siege of 1536 failed against about 190 Spanish defenders, Inca resistance withdrew to the Vilcabamba enclave instead of retaking the highlands. Had the siege succeeded, the Spanish would have lost their only foothold in the Inca heartland, and the course and pace of the conquest could have been very different. Spanish rule then remade the city without erasing it. Plots, churches and convents were set into Inca compounds, and the names of Inca neighbourhoods survived through the colonial era in notarial records and in local use. According to UNESCO, the colonial city became one of the continent's chief centres of religious art. Today Cusco is the clearest place to see Inca and Hispanic building layered in one plan, and Quechua-speaking people still treat it as sacred ground. It also faces present-day threats. UNESCO reports that tourism development is replacing historic houses and pushing original residents to the periphery. Seismologists warn that dense, unplanned growth now makes the basin more vulnerable to the faults that damaged it in 1650 and 1950.

beats.caption: Reconstruction: in the 15th century the town is rebuilt on one plan, from the Coricancha in the lower city to Saqsaywaman on the hill. Chronicles credit Pachacuti.
From the main plaza the Qhapaq Ñan runs out to the four suyus, binding the provinces of Tawantinsuyu to their capital.
15 November 1533 (Julian): Pizarro's main force enters Cusco; a month later the Spanish install Manco Inca as ruler.
From 1534 Spaniards take house plots inside the royal compounds around Haukaypata; Inca families are pushed out to the barrios.
May 1536: Manco Inca besieges the city. Heated sling-stones set thatch roofs alight and Saqsaywaman changes hands.
The ten-month siege fails; Manco withdraws to Vilcabamba, where a neo-Inca state survives beyond Spanish control.
31 March 1650: an earthquake devastates Cusco; the NOAA catalogue assigns the city intensity 10 (X).
By the 17th century, Santo Domingo stands over the Coricancha and Santa Catalina over the Acllahuasi, built on Inca walls.
21 May 1950: a magnitude 6.0 (Ms) earthquake strikes Cusco; the NOAA catalogue counts 129 dead and 265 injured.
1983: UNESCO inscribes the City of Cuzco (142.48 ha). Today tourism development is replacing old houses and moving residents to the edges.

perspectives.holder: Chronicle chronology: Cabello Valboa (1586) as systematised by Rowe (1945), long followed by most archaeologists and by museum timelines
perspectives.account: Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui took power in 1438, and that year marks the start of Inca conquests beyond the Cuzco valley.

perspectives.holder: Radiocarbon studies: Burger et al. (2021); Marsh et al. (2017); summarised by Covey et al. (2025)
perspectives.account: Machu Picchu, linked to Pachacuti, was occupied from about AD 1420, and Bayesian models place Inca occupation in Mendoza at cal AD 1350–1440 and at Chamical (Ecuador) at cal AD 1410–1480, so imperial expansion began decades before the chronicle dates. Covey et al. add that radiocarbon dating may refine, not overturn, the dynastic sequence.

The Inca capital grew out of a long regional process after AD 1000 and an earlier Killke settlement, rather than being the creation of a single ruler; Pachacuti's replanning is one stage in that history.

perspectives.holder: Inca origin tradition as recorded in Spanish chronicles (belief; legendary)
perspectives.account: The ruling line descended from Manco Capac, the first Inca, who emerged at Tambotoco near Pacariqtambo; later tradition tied the city's founding to his reign, placed by one reference work around 1200. Bauer argues the Cuzco elite built Maukallaqta near Pacariqtambo to honour this mythical ancestor.

perspectives.holder: Mar and Beltrán-Caballero (2014), following Cieza de León and others
perspectives.account: Saqsaywaman was less a fortress than the Sun House of upper Cusco, a ceremonial counterpart to the Coricancha that also stored arms. Spanish observers called it a fortress, and its zigzag walls still read as military.

15th-century replanning as the capital of Tawantinsuyu, credited to Pachacuti: Coricancha, royal compounds, plazas and Saqsaywaman as one planned whole. Start year is approximate: chronicles give 1438, radiocarbon points earlier.
Inca city at Spanish arrival; Saqsaywaman's zigzag walls still unfinished.
Spanish municipality founded; house plots assigned inside royal compounds such as Amarucancha; Acllahuasi residents protected by order.
Siege of Cusco: thatch roofs burned by heated sling-stones; fighting at Saqsaywaman.
Churches, monasteries and manor houses built over Inca walls, mostly Baroque with local adaptations.
Earthquake of 31 March 1650 devastates the colonial city.
Rebuilding; by the 17th century Santo Domingo stands over the Coricancha and Santa Catalina over the Acllahuasi.
Earthquake of 21 May 1950 damages about half the buildings; Inca masonry suffers only a few new fractures.
World Heritage inscription (1983); conservation under way while tourism development alters historic houses.
